q: The light emitted by hydrogen gas at low pressure in a discharge tube, when passed through a prism or grating, is seen to consist of:
o: A continuous band of all colours
A single bright line of one wavelength
A continuous band crossed by dark lines
Separate bright lines at definite wavelengths
x: A hot gas at low pressure gives an emission line spectrum: a set of separate bright lines whose wavelengths are characteristic of the element. A continuous band crossed by dark lines is an absorption spectrum.

q: Atoms give line spectra rather than continuous spectra because:
o: Electrons in atoms can have only certain discrete energies, so only photons of certain energies are emitted
Electrons in atoms can have any energy, so they emit all wavelengths
The nucleus emits photons of a few fixed wavelengths
Atoms emit light only when they collide with the walls of the tube
x: The energy levels of an atom are quantised. A photon is emitted when an electron drops between two levels, with hf equal to the energy gap, so only certain frequencies appear as lines.

q: When white light passes through a cool gas and is then dispersed, the absorption spectrum seen is:
o: Bright lines on a dark background
A continuous band of colours with no lines
A dark background with no lines
Dark lines on a continuous coloured background
x: Gas atoms absorb photons whose energies match their energy-level gaps, removing those wavelengths from the white light. Dark lines therefore appear on the otherwise continuous spectrum.

q: Each dark line in the absorption spectrum of a gas lies at a wavelength that:
o: Also appears as a bright line in the emission spectrum of the same gas
Is always longer than every line in its emission spectrum
Is always shorter than every line in its emission spectrum
Has no connection with its emission spectrum
x: A photon absorbed in a jump between two levels has the same energy as the photon emitted in the reverse jump. So each absorption line matches a line in the element's emission spectrum.

q: An electron in an atom falls from a level of energy E₂ to a lower level of energy E₁. The frequency f of the emitted photon is given by:
x: The photon carries away exactly the energy lost by the electron, so hf = E₂ − E₁. The energy is divided by h, not multiplied by it, to get f.

q: In a hydrogen atom an electron falls from the level of −3.4 eV to the level of −13.6 eV. What is the energy of the emitted photon?
x: Photon energy = E₂ − E₁ = (−3.4) − (−13.6) = 10.2 eV. Adding the magnitudes gives 17.0 eV, which is wrong.

q: In which region of the electromagnetic spectrum does the Lyman series of hydrogen lie?
x: Lyman lines come from falls to n = 1, which involve large energy gaps (10.2 eV or more), so the photons are in the ultraviolet.

q: Which series of hydrogen spectral lines lies in the visible region?
x: The Balmer series (falls to n = 2) gives the visible lines of hydrogen. Lyman lies in the ultraviolet; Paschen and Brackett lie in the infrared.

q: The Paschen series of hydrogen lies in the:
x: Paschen lines come from falls to n = 3, where the energy gaps are small, so the photons have long wavelengths in the infrared.

q: The lines of the Lyman series of hydrogen are produced when electrons fall from higher levels to the level:
x: Lyman lines end on n = 1 (the ground state), Balmer on n = 2, Paschen on n = 3 and Brackett on n = 4.

q: The red line of hydrogen's visible spectrum (wavelength 656 nm), the first Balmer line, is produced by which transition?
x: Balmer lines end on n = 2, and the longest-wavelength (red) one comes from the smallest fall, from n = 3. A fall to n = 1 would be in the ultraviolet.

q: An electron in a hydrogen atom falls from n = 5 to n = 3. The emitted line belongs to the:
x: The series is named by the final level: falls ending on n = 3 form the Paschen series, in the infrared.

q: The energy levels of hydrogen are given by Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. What is the energy of the level n = 2?
x: E₂ = −13.6 ÷ 2² = −13.6 ÷ 4 = −3.4 eV. Forgetting to square n gives −6.8 eV; −1.51 eV is the n = 3 level.

q: How much energy is needed to remove the electron completely from a hydrogen atom in its ground state (−13.6 eV)?
x: The electron must be raised from −13.6 eV to 0 eV (n = ∞), which needs 13.6 eV, the ionisation energy of hydrogen. 10.2 eV only lifts it to n = 2.

q: The energies of the electron levels in an atom are given negative values because:
o: Zero energy is taken for a free electron at infinity, and a bound electron has less energy than that
The electron loses energy continuously while it orbits
Energy levels nearer the nucleus have more energy than those far away
x: A free electron at rest far from the nucleus has zero energy; energy must be supplied to free a bound electron, so bound levels are below zero. The sign has nothing to do with the electron's charge.

q: In an X-ray tube, X-rays are produced when:
o: Light falls on a metal surface
Fast-moving electrons strike a target of a heavy metal
A metal target is heated strongly
x: Electrons from the hot filament are accelerated through a high voltage and stopped by a heavy-metal target such as tungsten; part of their energy comes out as X-rays. Light on a metal gives the photoelectric effect.

q: Electrons in an X-ray tube are accelerated through 25 kV. What is the maximum energy of an X-ray photon produced (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)?
x: The most energetic photon takes all of an electron's kinetic energy: E = eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.5 × 10⁴ = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. Taking 25 kV as 25 V gives a value a thousand times smaller.

q: An X-ray tube works at 20 kV. Taking h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, what is the shortest wavelength of the X-rays produced?
x: eV = hc/λmin, so λmin = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2 × 10⁴) = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁵/3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ ≈ 6.2 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Using 20 V instead of 20 kV gives 6.2 × 10⁻⁸ m.

q: The accelerating voltage of an X-ray tube is doubled. The shortest wavelength in the X-ray spectrum:
x: λmin = hc/eV, inversely proportional to V, so doubling V halves λmin. The photons get more energetic, so their wavelength cannot increase.

q: The filament current of an X-ray tube is increased while the accelerating voltage is kept the same. What happens to the X-rays?
o: Their intensity increases but their shortest wavelength is unchanged
x: More filament current releases more electrons per second, so more X-ray photons are made (greater intensity), but each electron still gains only eV, so λmin and the penetrating power are unchanged. The voltage controls λmin.

q: The Kα line in the characteristic X-ray spectrum of a target is emitted when an electron in a target atom:
o: Falls from the M shell into a vacancy in the L shell
Is slowed down by the electric field of a nucleus
Moves from the K shell up to the L shell
Falls from the L shell into a vacancy in the K shell
x: After a K-shell electron is knocked out, an electron from the next shell (L) drops in and emits a Kα photon. Slowing of electrons near nuclei gives the continuous spectrum, and moving upward absorbs energy.

q: In the target metal of an X-ray tube, the K-shell energy is −70 keV and the L-shell energy is −12 keV. What is the smallest accelerating voltage at which the K-series lines can appear?
x: A K line needs a vacancy in the K shell, so an electron must knock a K electron right out of the atom, which needs 70 keV: a voltage of at least 70 kV. 58 keV is the energy of the Kα photon itself, not the energy to make the vacancy.

q: Bones show up clearly in an X-ray photograph of the hand because:
o: Bone reflects X-rays back into the tube
Bone absorbs X-rays more strongly than the soft tissue around it
X-rays are bent by bone onto the film
Soft tissue gives out X-rays of its own
x: Bone contains heavier elements such as calcium and absorbs more X-rays, so less radiation reaches the film behind it and it appears as a light shadow. X-rays pass through, they are not reflected or focused.

q: The word LASER stands for:
o: Light Absorption by Spontaneous Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation
Light Amplification by Spontaneous Emission of Rays
Low-energy Amplification by Stimulated Electron Radiation
x: LASER = Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. The key process is stimulated emission, not spontaneous emission or absorption.

q: Laser action needs a population inversion. This means that:
o: All the atoms are in the ground state
Atoms are ionised and electrons move freely
The atoms move in the direction opposite to the light
More atoms are in an excited state than in the lower state to which they fall
x: Normally most atoms are in the lower state, so photons are absorbed more than they stimulate emission. With more atoms in the upper state, stimulated emission wins and the light is amplified.

q: Laser materials use a metastable state. Its importance is that:
o: Atoms in it cannot emit light at all
It is the ground state of the atom
Atoms stay in it much longer (about 10⁻³ s) than in an ordinary excited state, so a population inversion can build up
x: Ordinary excited states last about 10⁻⁸ s; a metastable state lasts far longer, so excited atoms pile up there faster than they decay and a population inversion forms.

q: In stimulated emission, a photon causes an excited atom to emit a second photon. Compared with the first photon, the emitted photon has:
o: The same frequency, phase and direction
The same frequency but a random direction
x: The stimulated photon is an exact copy of the incoming one: same energy (frequency), phase and direction. This is why laser light is coherent, monochromatic and narrow. Random direction and phase belong to spontaneous emission.

q: In a helium-neon laser, the laser light is emitted by neon atoms. What is the role of the helium atoms?
o: They emit the red laser light
They are excited by the discharge and pass their energy to neon atoms by collisions
They absorb the laser light to keep it narrow
They act as the mirrors of the laser
x: Helium atoms excited by the electric discharge collide with neon atoms and transfer energy to a neon level of almost the same energy, giving a population inversion in neon; neon then emits the 632.8 nm light.

q: A laser emits light of wavelength 663 nm with a power of 3 mW. Taking h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, how many photons does it emit per second?
x: Photon energy E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(6.63 × 10⁻⁷) = 3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; number per second = P/E = 3 × 10⁻³/3 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1 × 10¹⁶. Taking 3 mW as 3 W gives 1 × 10¹⁹.

q: Hydrogen levels are −13.6 eV (n = 1), −3.4 eV (n = 2) and −1.51 eV (n = 3). An electron with 12 eV of kinetic energy collides with a hydrogen atom in its ground state. The electron can:
o: Not excite the atom at all
Excite the atom to n = 2 only
x: Excitation to n = 2 needs 10.2 eV and to n = 3 needs 12.09 eV, so 12 eV is enough only for n = 2; ionisation needs 13.6 eV. Unlike a photon, an electron can give up only part of its energy, so the 1.8 eV left over stays with it.
